reading.title: Two Notebooks at the Science Fair
reading.purpose: Watch how two reporters describe the exact same gym event from different angles.
paras: The school gym smelled of cardboard, glue, and buttered popcorn as judges walked past rows of science fair boards. From the bleachers, Maya had a wide vantage, a high position that let her see every table at once. Beside her sat Devon, who was writing for the school paper. Their teacher had asked both students to cover the afternoon, yet each one brought a different point of view to the assignment.

Maya wanted her report to be strictly objective, built only on facts anyone could verify with a notebook and a camera. She counted forty-two projects, timed the judges' rounds, and quoted two winners word for word. Her tone stayed detached, standing apart from the excitement so that no personal feeling colored her lines. When she tried to characterize the winning display, she listed its clean wiring, clear charts, and steady water pump.

Devon sat down among the contestants instead of up in the stands. His notebook grew intimate as he wrote down quiet whispers, nervous jokes, and the tight grip a seventh grader kept on a model bridge. Because Devon's younger sister had entered a volcano project, his notes quickly turned subjective, shaped by family pride rather than plain facts. He was clearly partial to his sister's table, praising her paint job while skipping the flawed data chart beside it.

When they compared drafts after the awards, Maya pointed out that an unreliable narrator leaves out details that do not fit a favorite story. Devon laughed and admitted he had left out the moment his sister's pump jammed. "Even if we were omniscient and knew every thought in the gym," Maya said, "we would still have to choose which facts to share." Devon reopened his notebook and began adding the missing numbers beside his favorite quotes.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "detached" most nearly means
choices: excited about cheering for a close friend or family member
standing apart without letting strong feelings guide the writing
missing key facts because the writer arrived too late to see
knowing every secret thought inside every person in the room
qs.why: Paragraph 2 explains that Maya's tone stayed detached by "standing apart from the excitement so that no personal feeling colored her lines."

qs.q: Which sentence shows why Devon's notes favored one project over the others?
choices: Devon sat down among the contestants instead of up in the stands.
His notebook grew intimate as he wrote down quiet whispers, nervous jokes, and the tight grip a seventh grader kept on a model bridge.
Because Devon's younger sister had entered a volcano project, his notes quickly turned subjective, shaped by family pride rather than plain facts.
He was clearly partial to his sister's table, praising her paint job while skipping the flawed data chart beside it.
qs.why: This sentence names the exact cause of his bias: his younger sister had entered a project, so family pride shaped his notes.

ev.text: Because Devon's younger sister had entered a volcano project, his notes quickly turned subjective, shaped by family pride rather than plain facts.

qs.q: Why does Devon add the missing numbers to his notebook at the end?
choices: He wants to replace Maya as the main photographer for the school paper.
He realizes that leaving out flaws made his report unfair and incomplete.
He decides that personal quotes should never appear in any news story.
He hopes the judges will recount the scores for his sister's display.
qs.why: After Maya explains how an unreliable narrator omits inconvenient details, Devon admits skipping the jammed pump and adds the missing numbers.

qs.q: What is the central idea of this story?
choices: Reporters should always sit in the highest bleachers when covering a busy school event.
Science fair judges only reward projects that have clean wiring and steady water pumps.
A writer's position and feelings shape a report, so checking for missing facts matters.
Family members should never be allowed to attend or write about the same school contest.
qs.why: The story contrasts Maya's distant, fact-based vantage with Devon's close, biased notes and concludes that writers must still share fair facts.

clues.text: a high position that let her see every table at once
built only on facts anyone could verify
shaped by family pride rather than plain facts
knew every thought in the gym
